title: Devadatta
hookLine: the cousin who wanted to lead the order

cards: The Vinaya puts Devadatta in good company. A group of young Sakyan nobles leave home together to follow the Buddha: Anuruddha, Ananda, Bhaddiya and others, with the barber Upali alongside. Devadatta is one of them.

Tradition remembers him as the Buddha's cousin. For a while his story runs like theirs. Then, the text says, he starts to wonder whom he could win over, someone whose favor would bring him gain and honor.
He chooses a prince, Ajatasattu, the king's son. Today, what Devadatta wanted next.

teach.b: First, the patron. Devadatta impresses the young prince with a show of power, and the prince begins sending him food, morning and evening, in carts. Gain and honor pour in.
Second, the request. Then Devadatta goes to the Buddha, in front of a large gathering, and says: you're old now, Lord. Live at ease.
Hand the order of monks over to me, and I'll lead it. Third, the refusal. The Buddha says no.
I wouldn't hand the order over even to Sariputta and Moggallana, he says, let alone to you. The words are sharp, and spoken in public.
The text says Devadatta left angry and displeased, and that this was the first grudge he held against the Buddha. Fourth, the warning.
Elsewhere in the canon the Buddha says gain, honor and praise came to Devadatta for his own ruin, the way a banana plant bears fruit and then dies, or a bamboo or a reed fruits and is finished.

In the story, the trouble isn't leading itself: other disciples taught, guided and looked after the monks. What the text holds up is the wish to take charge, fed by carts of food and a prince's favor.

how: Buddhist teachers tell Devadatta's story as a warning about gain, honor and ambition inside a spiritual community.

games.q: you're the Buddha. in front of everyone, Devadatta says: you're old now; hand the order over to me. what do you do?
games.why: he refuses: not even to Sariputta and Moggallana, let alone to Devadatta. Devadatta leaves angry, holding his first grudge.

practice: Look back over the last day or two for a moment when you wanted the final say, in a meeting, a group chat, at home.

That's ordinary; now look closer at what fed it, getting things right, helping people, or being seen as the one, and there may be some of each. Don't judge it; just name it, and let the breath carry on.

wordCard.voice: Devadatta. A Sakyan monk, remembered as the Buddha's cousin, who grew rich in gain and honor and asked to be handed the order. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali labhasakkara: gain and honor, which the Buddha says came to Devadatta for his ruin.

carryVoice: Your line: the wish to lead. Gain and honor came first; the grudge came after. Until tomorrow.
